sections.h2: Where is Tupelo, Mississippi, and how big is it?
sections.html:
Tupelo is the county seat of Lee County in northeast Mississippi, roughly midway between Memphis and Birmingham. It had 37,923 residents at the 2020 census, making it the seventh-most populous city in the state and a commercial and industrial hub for the region.

The city covers about 51 square miles and sits on Interstate 22 and U.S. Route 78. The wider Tupelo micropolitan area includes Lee, Itawamba and Pontotoc counties. Most sellers deal with two governments: the City of Tupelo for permits and code, and Lee County for property tax.

The 2020 census counted 17,102 housing units in the city, with 9.5 percent vacant. The homeowner vacancy rate was 1.5 percent and the rental vacancy rate was 13.3 percent.

sections.h2: What is Tupelo's history, and why does the 1936 tornado still matter?
sections.html:
Tupelo grew up as a railroad settlement called Gum Pond, took its present name after the 1864 Battle of Tupelo, and was incorporated on July 20, 1870. In 1934 it became the first city to receive power from the Tennessee Valley Authority, which is why it is nicknamed the First TVA City.

On April 5 and 6, 1936, a tornado outbreak leveled 48 city blocks and more than 200 homes and killed 216 people, mostly on the north side, according to the figures cited on Wikipedia. The storm has since been rated F5. More recent tornadoes include an EF3 on May 8, 2008, another large EF3 on April 28, 2014, and a May 2, 2021 tornado that struck the northwest side of downtown.

For a house seller, the takeaway is practical. Tupelo has a documented tornado history, so a patched roof or a repaired wall is likely to draw questions in an inspection, and a seller with repair paperwork ready can answer them quickly.

sections.h2: What does Tupelo's economy mean for local homeowners?
sections.html:
Tupelo's economy rests on health care, banking, retail, manufacturing and tourism. North Mississippi Medical Center is headquartered here and is described as the largest non-metropolitan hospital in the United States.

  • Cadence Bank and Renasant Bank are both headquartered in Tupelo. Wikipedia notes that it is the smallest U.S. city hosting more than one bank with over $10 billion in assets.
  • Furniture manufacturing was long a major industry in northeast Mississippi, and companies such as Tecumseh, Heritage Home Group and Cooper Tire have operated in Tupelo and Lee County.
  • Toyota's Mississippi plant is in nearby Blue Springs, selected in 2007.
  • Tourism centers on the Elvis Presley Birthplace and the Natchez Trace Parkway, whose headquarters is in Tupelo.

Wikipedia notes that many of Tupelo's manufacturing industries have declined since the 1990s, while health care, retail and financial services have kept the city growing. A household's job mix can therefore differ a lot from one neighborhood to the next, and sellers should not assume a single trend applies to their street.

sections.h2: What should a Tupelo seller know about permits, rentals and code enforcement?
sections.html:
The City of Tupelo's Department of Development Services handles permits, building, planning and code enforcement, and it does not approve permits without a current recorded deed. Permitting staff can be reached at 662-841-6510 or permits@tupeloms.gov, and the office is on the third floor of City Hall at 71 East Troy Street.

Code Enforcement helps owners comply with the city's ordinances and Development Code, and owners are responsible for keeping property in compliance. A letter of violation or citation has to be resolved with that office, and fines can follow if it is not. The city publishes a rental inspection checklist and property maintenance standards, and its Building Division runs a Blight and Demolition Program.

  • Check for open violations before you list, since they can surface in a buyer's due diligence.
  • If you rent the house, ask Permitting about the rental inspection process.
  • Gather permits for past work, because the city requires a recorded deed with any application.

Parts of Tupelo fall inside historic and design overlay districts, including the downtown historic district and the Fairpark redevelopment district, which have their own design standards. Anyone planning exterior changes near downtown should ask Planning first.

sections.h2: How are Lee County property taxes and homestead exemption handled?
sections.html:
Lee County bills the tax, and it is due on or before February 1 for property assessed the preceding year. The Tax Collector can be reached at 662-432-2200 (mailing address PO Box 271, Tupelo, MS 38802), and the Tax Assessor at 662-432-2700.

A single-family, owner-occupied home is Class I and assessed at 10 percent of true value, while other real property is Class II at 15 percent. Real property is revalued at least every four years. Homestead exemption must be applied for with the Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1, and it generally needs a recorded warranty deed, Social Security numbers and the cost of the home. The Lee County Homestead Office number is 662-432-2706.

The exemption follows the owner. The regular tier is a credit of up to $300, and people 65 or older or totally disabled are exempt on the first $7,500 of assessed value. A buyer must own and occupy the house as a primary residence on January 1, with the deed filed with the Chancery Clerk before January 7.

Delinquent property taxes are the other thing to check. The Lee County Tax Collector's office posts a last day to pay real property taxes before the August tax sale, and the Tax Assessor's FAQ says that after a lien is sold the owner has two years to pay the taxes plus interest at 1.5 percent per month through the Chancery Clerk.

sections.h2: What does Mississippi require when you sell a Tupelo house, and what are your options?
sections.html:
Mississippi Code Section 89-1-503 requires the seller to give the buyer a written property condition disclosure statement as soon as practicable before title transfers. If the buyer receives it after making an offer, the buyer has three days after hand delivery or five days after mailing to cancel in writing.

Tupelo sellers usually choose among three routes: listing with an agent, selling to an investor, or selling directly to a cash buyer who purchases as is. Listing works when a house is in good repair and you can wait. A cash sale is often the more practical route for a house with storm damage, code violations, tax trouble or an estate with several heirs.

Whichever you pick, start with a title search by an attorney or title company, which will show liens and unpaid taxes and whether the seller holds legal title.

Cash Home Buyers speaks with Tupelo sellers about as-is purchases and explains the terms in writing before you decide, so you can compare them against listing.

faqs.q: Do I need a recorded deed to pull a permit in Tupelo?
faqs.a: Yes. The City of Tupelo says it approves no permits without a current recorded deed, and all applications require a completed application and a recorded deed.

faqs.q: When are Lee County property taxes due?
faqs.a: They are due on or before February 1 for property assessed the preceding year, with payment accepted the following Monday if February 1 falls on a weekend.
The Tupelo Public School District serves the vast majority of the city, and some parts of Tupelo are zoned to the Lee County School District.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Tupelo house that has code violations?
faqs.a: You can, but a violation letter or citation has to be resolved with Code Enforcement, and unresolved issues can surface in a buyer's inspection. A cash buyer purchasing as is will price the problem in.

faqs.q: How long do I have to redeem a house sold at a tax sale in Lee County?
faqs.a: The Lee County Tax Assessor's FAQ says the owner has two years from the purchase date to pay the taxes plus interest of 1.5 percent per month through the Chancery Clerk.
